#4794. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

#4793. The Universality of Privilege and Inheritance of Excellence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The word privilege has somehow evolved linguistically to be viewed negatively. It has also come to imply an unearned advantage or an unfair benefit held by one group at another's expense.

Throughout human history, privilege has meant something quite different: privilege has emerged when individuals and/or groups apply merit, achievement, competence, and excellence in ways that expand possibilities for everyone. I refer to this as the MACE Principle.

Research shows that high levels of expertize and exceptional performance emerge through sustained practice, learning, and skill refinement rather than arising spontaneously. In this sense, such accomplishments and the benefits they create for subsequent generations are among the oldest features of human civilization (Ericsson, 2008; Srivastava & Das, 2015).

Nearly three million years ago, our distant ancestors fashioned the first stone tools. The first person to shape stone into a cutting implement created something far more significant than a simple object. That innovation gave the entire group a practical advantage.

The collective also gained a privilege. The tribe could now cut hunted and gathered food and, self-evidently, share their food far more efficiently and much more quickly. Survival itself became easier.

Consequently, the privilege created by that stone-tool innovation was not confined to the inventor; it became a significant benefit and privilege enjoyed by the collective (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

The same pattern recurs throughout history. The invention of the wheel transformed transport and trade. Once developed, the wheel's benefits and the privilege it created extended far beyond its creator.

Entire communities far removed from the original invention gained the privilege of moving goods and people more efficiently. What began as an achievement of human ingenuity became a shared privilege and an immense social advantage beyond its original location (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

Perhaps no invention demonstrates this process more dramatically than the printing press. Developed in the 15th century by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, within the Holy Roman Empire (present-day Germany), the printing press fundamentally altered humanity's relationship with the development and advancement of knowledge.

Reading, writing, collective information, ideas, and knowledge, once largely confined to a comparatively small number of individuals, could now be reproduced, preserved, and distributed on a scale that was never before possible.

Reading and writing ceased to be “a mystery” for a select number of individuals or a “select” group. As with the stone tool and the wheel before it, the printing press created new benefits and privileges, consequently moving these benefits and privileges from the few to the many.

Although history informs us (as with all inventions and achievements), the resulting benefits and privileges were not always distributed equally.

However, even with this being the case, with the wider dissemination of knowledge (following the invention of the 15th-century printing press), the benefits of this invention extended far beyond Gutenberg and transformed what future generations could achieve (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

Consider what followed. For approximately three million years, humanity crafted tools, built settlements, established civilizations, constructed cities, developed metallurgy, crossed oceans, fought wars, and created empires.

During this period, countless innovations delivered immense benefits and privilege. Yet the accumulation and transmission of knowledge remained comparatively limited.

Then, within about five centuries of the invention of the printing press, humanity witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in the growth and development of knowledge (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In the 18th century, Edward Jenner laid the foundations of modern immunization with the first successful smallpox vaccination (Riedel, 2005).

In the 20th century, the United States sent three men to the Moon: Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on its surface; Buzz Aldrin, the second; and Michael Collins, who remained in lunar orbit as part of the mission.

These achievements produced further benefits and privilege, as earlier innovations had. They reflected humanity's expanding capacity to preserve, transmit, and build upon knowledge. The printing press transformed reading, writing, ideas, and information into a far more widely shared social benefit and privilege for the many (Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In doing so, it expanded the benefits and privilege available to successive generations and helped create the conditions for scientific, technological, and civilizational advancement to proceed at a pace previously unknown in human history (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

The same principle applied across medicine, engineering, agriculture, chemistry, and countless other fields.

Vaccines, clean water systems, supermarkets, automobiles, telecommunications, digital technologies, and now artificial intelligence all exist because individuals pursued excellence in their respective domains.

The benefits of those achievements are enjoyed not merely by their creators but by millions, and even potentially billions, of people (Tewksbury et al., 1980; Yu & Liu, 2021).

Throughout history, parents have generally sought to provide advantages, opportunities, benefits, and privilege to their children, just as previous generations sought to provide them to those who followed.

Civilization itself can therefore be understood as the cumulative result of countless individuals attempting to improve the circumstances inherited by the next generation (Gulyas & Powell, 2019; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

This does not self-evidently mean that every benefit or privilege is distributed equally; it never has and it never will.

It does mean, however, that inventions and achievements, no matter what they were, enriched lives, from the smallest tribes to the largest civilizations, because there were individuals who invented something that changed what previously existed, and with this, benefits and privilege arose (Dean et al., 2014; Tewksbury et al., 1980).

The story of human civilization is the story of expanding everyone's potential for privilege, but not a guarantee. Through innovation, discovery, and excellence, however, humanity has repeatedly turned extraordinary achievements into benefits that potentially eventually become available to the broader populace.

The greatest privilege is that each generation inherits the achievements of those who came before and can contribute new ones for those yet to come (Dean et al., 2014; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

#4792. Volkswagen’s affordable ID. Polo wins German Car of the Year 2027 as EVs dominate

Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo took the overall title of “German Car of the Year 2027,” starting at just €24,995 ($28,000).

After winning in its class among entry-level models (up to €25,000), the VW ID. Polo beat out strong international competition to take the top spot as German Car of the Year for 2027 among all vehicles.

The Volkswagen Group has won two years in a row with a compact EV. Last year, it was the Skoda Elroq.

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April. In July, it added the entry-level model with the 37 kWh battery, starting at just €24,995 ($28,000) with a WLTP range of up to 207 miles (334 km).

The Life and Style variants are also available with the 37 kWh battery, starting from €29,195 ($32,500).

With DC fast charging speeds of up to 90 kW, the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes.

The prestigious award “confirms what the ID. Polo stands for,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said. He added the entry-level EV “brings electric mobility to where it can make the greatest impact: right into people’s everyday lives.”

Since orders opened at the end of April, Schäfer said “well over 50,000 people have ordered their ID. Polo.”

As the first of what the company calls “a true Volkswagen again,” the ID. Polo is the first to bear an established name and the brand’s new Pure Positive design language.

The jury includes nearly 50 German and international auto journalists, and the award is considered one of the most prestigious in the industry.

The reason this class of vehicles is winning awards is that Europe buys a lot of B-segment vehicles (small hatchbacks) that aren't intended as city-only transport. Many families use them as their only vehicle.

And, up till now, there haven't been many BEVs available in that category.

It is compact, reasonably powerful, reasonably fast charging, acceptable charging rate, has good luggage capacity and feels nice to drive.

In other segments, electric cars swept the awards, with the Kia PV5 van winning in the compact class (€25,000 and €40,000), and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric taking the top spot in the premium segment (€40,000 to €70,000). Hyundai’s electric sports car, the IONIQ 6 N, won German Performance Car 2027.

Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss, said earlier this month the company is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market.

VW Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June. The lineup currently includes the VW ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the MEB+ platform.

While those in the US won’t see the entry-level ID. Polo, Volkswagen is set to launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

#4791. The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Reshaping People’s Looks—And Not in a Flattering Way

WHEN YOU LOSE weight through traditional diet and exercise, you tend to see a gradual slimming down of your face. But when you add in gray-market peptides like retatrutide, you’re expediting the weight loss process. That also includes rapid fat loss in the face, leaving a sunken and hollowed-out look people are dubbing “reta face.”

Online Reddit communities on peptides and biohacking are packed with people commenting on changes to their facial appearance after taking retatrutide—a triple hormone agonist of the GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors that’s expected to become the next generation of weight-loss injections. One clinical trial found those taking retatrutide had more than double the weight loss of people taking Ozempic.

To be fair, “Ozempic face” has also been an issue. But with Eli Lilly expected to apply for FDA approval of retatrutide in early 2027 for obesity and other conditions, doctors say reta will likely cause more facial volume issues. Is there any way to prevent these unflattering side effects? We went straight to the doctors currently treating people with facial symptoms from GLPs.

WHILE RETA FACE isn’t an official medical diagnosis, it’s a real phenomenon. “The facial changes can be kind of dramatic,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. But the lack of criteria has also caused some debate over what qualifies as reta face.

On the r/BodyHackGuide community (with over 87,000 contributors dubbed “Lab Rats”), reta face before-and-after posts are recurring discussion threads. Some describe reta face as a chiseled look after weight loss while Ozempic face is the more sickly face. Others argue that “reta face” and “Ozempic face” are simply two terms to describe the sunken look from your face losing fat.

“Reta face is the new Ozempic face,” says dermatologist Gary Goldenberg, MD. “Since retatrutide is a triple biologic agonist that produces more significant weight loss than GLP peptides, patients may have an even more exaggerated appearance of a sunken, aged look.”

That means cheeks can become flat and hollow, temples narrow, and undereye areas can look sunken and dark. “Facial bones can also become more prominent as fat disappears,” says Dr. Goldenberg. “The skin can thin, as collagen and elastic fibers have less underlying fat plumping them up.”

Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research in dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital, says the shape of your face changes with any significant weight loss—it’s just more apparent when someone is on a weight-loss medication.

ABSOLUTELY. DR. ZEICHNER says minimizing the appearance of facial wasting is all about losing weight slowly—even when taking a GLP-1 or reta. While you can’t target specific areas for fat loss, Dr. Goldenberg recommends pacing yourself while still getting plenty of protein on your plate and being selective about meals that have enough nutrients.

If you already have reta face and the appearance bothers you, Dr. Goldenberg recommends seeing a dermatologist. “Collagen stimulators and fillers are a very common treatment for this problem,” he says. “Volume can be restored and contouring can be improved with these treatments.”

#4790. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4788. What Perpetuates the Family Cycle of Violence?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

This post is the second in an occasional series on the family cycle of violence.

In May 2026, we posted "Do Abused Parents Become Child Abusers?" which we subtitled: "Multiple interacting factors shape the intergenerational cycle of maltreatment." That post is intended to be the foundation for an undetermined number of future posts examining the intergenerational transmission of increased risk for maltreatment to the offspring of parents who were maltreated themselves as children. The larger focus of this series is the two-part question: “Can we break the family cycle of violence?” and “If so, how?”

The key points of the earlier post are that the single most powerful risk factor for a child being maltreated is having a parent who was maltreated. Most (~70 percent) parents with child maltreatment histories do not become abusive parents. However, the risk of becoming an abusive parent is 6 to 12 times higher than for parents without a childhood maltreatment history. The mechanisms underlying this increased risk may be indirect (e.g., decreased parental vigilance) or direct (perpetration). This increased risk is a result of multiple, interacting levels of factors (e.g., depression, dissociation, substance abuse, domestic violence, unsafe households, poverty, neighborhood factors, public policies). To be cost-effective, prevention programs must seek to address the most critical shared underlying factors synergistically.

The post also notes that individuals can promote positive social change by openly acknowledging their own and others’ childhood maltreatment, thereby validating survivors, reducing stigma, and keeping public attention focused on this enormous public health problem.

How do we tease out the most critical factors on which to focus the always limited prevention resources? This conundrum is further complicated by the need to follow these multiple interacting factors in large general population samples for decades. Not to mention that even the most dedicated family violence researchers are lifetime-limited to studying only two or three generations during their careers.

There is another way, however, to get at least a ballpark understanding of the interacting factors that promote the family cycle of violence across generations. This involves the use of Agent-Based Models. ABMs are computer simulations in which individual “people” are represented by computational entities (agents) that can behave and interact with each other according to predefined rules (Smaldino, 2023). Think SimCity or other computer games that involve characters with past histories, have current and future agendas, and develop complicated interrelationships that can evolve apart and together “over time” to produce a range of outcomes.

Computer simulations, both equation-based and agent-based, are widely used to investigate systems and processes that are too large, too complex, and too costly to study on real-world scales. Examples include the weather, epidemics, and the Big Bang. One advantage is that computer simulations can be run thousands of times as needed to sweep through the numerous combinations of potential variables, searching for fundamental trajectories, collapses, singularities, best fits with real-world data, and critical tipping points that may serve as prevention targets.

Perhaps the best way to understand an ABM is to briefly describe a model simulating the intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The model begins with a number of unmarried adult males and females (typically 50 each to limit CPU time, as this breeds hundreds of new agents over three to five generations). These male and female adults are randomly scattered on a multicolored checkerboard “city” map of neighborhoods that hold different levels of risk for children born in them.

In generation 0, each agent (males are blue, females green) is randomly assigned a lifespan and a level of positive and negative “childhood” baggage, some of which may be passed to offspring. These adults proceed to seek out an opposite-gender partner with which to have “children.” Each adult can “see” the childhood baggage of the adults immediately around them and chooses a partner based on a variable called “match” (more on “match” below).

If there is not a suitable “match” in sight, agents take off randomly seeking one. Some agents never meet their “match” and never have children. In addition, each agent is randomly assigned a lifespan at birth. When their lifespan is up, they die and are removed from the board.

When a pair of agents do match—that is, their combined childhood baggage is within the bounds set by the “match” variable—they can “marry,” and every so often they breed a child. They also move around as a family, landing in positive or negative neighborhoods, which affect their growing children. The children pass through three developmental stages (infancy, childhood, adolescence), eventually becoming adults who carry forward into the next generation the risk accumulated over their childhoods. Childhood risk may be concentrated at certain developmental stages or distributed randomly across development, with the weight that earlier acquired risk has a greater lifetime impact.

When the adolescents become young adults, they leave their families to seek a partner with which to have their own children. A new “generation” occurs when a specified percentage (typically 70 percent) of children born to the preceding generation have reached adulthood. Models are typically run for three to five generations, and a combination of inputs is examined for their effects on outputs such as percent of population abused, average risk scores, female-to-male victim ratios, or geographic density of abuse/non-abuse clusters.

A typical experiment involves sweeping through a pre-set combination of variables (e.g., threshold for domestic violence, gender sensitivity coefficients, degree of match) to see how various combinations affect selected outputs. Typically, each combination of inputs is run at least 100 times, and the results are saved to a file for detailed statistical analyses.

The “match” variable was included among the input parameters because of research on the nonrandom or “assortative” mating of individuals with mental health diagnoses. Epidemiologists have found that individuals with mental health diagnoses are significantly more likely to partner with mates who have the same or related diagnoses than are comparison subjects with medical diagnoses having similar degrees of lifestyle impact, such as diabetes or epilepsy. Large-scale Swedish studies have found the frequency of assortative mating for 11 major mental health conditions ranges between two and six times that of equivalent medical conditions (Nordsletten et al., 2016).

“All computer models are wrong, but some are useful” —Old programmer saying

Somewhat to my surprise, “match” has turned out to be a critical variable driving rates of intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The ABM finds that the impact of two parents with childhood maltreatment histories significantly increases the risk that their offspring will also suffer maltreatment. Much of this effect is driven by the increased rate of domestic violence found when both parents have a childhood maltreatment history.

Thus, among the potential insights gained from the ABM model is that a childhood history of maltreatment in both parents is potentially a major risk factor for continuation of the family cycle of violence. How often this double parental maltreatment history occurs in real life is difficult to establish at present. However, if we accept that the assortative mating research on psychiatric diagnoses also applies to some degree to individuals with trauma-associated psychiatric disorders, it could happen among a significant number of family violence cases.

Computer models are “thinking machines.” They require their authors to think through dynamic processes and to formulate and parameterize the resulting algorithms. An ABM model is not real life, but sometimes it can yield insights that would be impossible to glean from real life without investing many years and millions of dollars.

Smaldino, P.E. (2023). Modeling Social Behavior: Mathematical and Agent-Based Models of Social Dynamics and Cultural Evolution. Princeton University Press.

Nordsletten, A.E. et al. (2016) Patterns of Nonrandom Mating Within and Across 11 Major Psychiatric Disorders. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016;73(4):354–361.

#4787. The 7 Best Electric Toothbrushes for Men in 2026, Tested by Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Cleaner, healthier teeth with picks for every budget and style of brushing.

YOU ALREADY KNOW you need to brush at least twice a day, no matter what toothpaste or mouthwash you use. But technique matters just as much. Even for me—a grooming editor who writes about this stuff—it can feel like a chore. In the morning, I brush before coffee when I’m barely awake. At night, I’m wiped out from the day or drifting off for less wholesome reasons. That’s why I love electric toothbrushes: they simplify brushing and deliver a better clean by doing most of the work for you.

Unlike manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrushes use vibrations and automated head movement to remove plaque and debris. Many models include smart programs for whitening or gum care, interchangeable heads for sensitive or deep cleaning, and built-in timers. Some of the latest options even feature AI that tracks your brushing and suggests improvements.

But the main selling point of electric toothbrushes is their ability to clean more thoroughly and efficiently than manual options, using power and vibrations no hand can match. Top-tier electric toothbrushes can be pricey, but they’re an investment in your smile. It’s the closest you can get to a dentist-level clean at home.

For the past two years, the Oral-B Series 10 has been listed at the top of this list. It remains the best overall electric toothbrush; however, it’s currently sold out everywhere due to this demand. The model that immediately preceded it, the iO Series 9, is the next best thing. It features many of the same features and power, just with a less high-tech charging mount (which may be a benefit for some who prefer something lighter and less complicated).

Series 9 is similarly a premium electric toothbrush packed with advanced features designed to elevate your oral care routine. Just like the 10, there are seven customizable modes—including Daily Clean, Sensitive, Super Sensitive, Intense, Gum Care, Tongue Clean, and Whitening—this brush adapts to your needs, whether you have sensitive gums or want a deep clean. Its oscillating, vibrating round brush head provides a powerful yet gentle clean, and the built-in pressure sensor ensures you're brushing with the right amount of force, lighting up red (too strong), blue (too weak), or green (just right) based on your pressure.

The Series 9 pairs with a companion app to track your brushing in real time across 16 zones of the mouth, offering instant feedback and a visual map of missed areas. I’m not a huge tech junkie, especially when it comes to something like brushing my teeth, since I just want to get it over with quickly. But this is one of the few apps that genuinely adds value, with accurate tracking, clear visuals, and brushing reminders.

Even if you skip the app, the built-in display shows your selected mode and a timer, though the latter is easier to read in the app. That being said, it’s nearly impossible to achieve a 100 percent clean according to the app (I usually aim for between 80 and 90) without brushing for five or more minutes, which is not recommended because it can damage enamel. If you’re a perfectionist, this will prove annoying.

In terms of design, the Series 9 is sleek and solid, and comes with a sturdy travel case. It charges in just three hours (significantly faster than most others on this list) and comes with four replacement heads, which should cover your first year of use if you replace them every three months, as dentists advise.

If you prefer sonic, this toothbrush offers nearly the same level of features and effectiveness as the Oral-B iO Series 9. At $340, it's also one of the most expensive electric toothbrushes, but the price includes five modes and three intensity settings to fully customize your brushing experience, along with an innovative charging cup.

Interchangeable brush heads, specifically designed for tasks like whitening or tongue cleaning, also help you achieve optimal results with minimal effort. Similar to the Series 9, it also has app-enabled smart modes that provide personalized feedback on your brushing habits and overall progress. Plus, the charging travel case makes it easy to travel while protecting your investment.

Women’s Health Associate Style and Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz has been using this toothbrush for the past year and says it’s the cleanest her teeth have ever felt. “I’ve long been using an electric toothbrush, so I didn’t expect to be too blown away by this one. I was wrong.” She likes how it pairs multiple brush heads, cleaning modes, and a timer with real-time app feedback to keep her brushing technique on track. The sleek charging cup also makes storage and charging effortless, even on a tiny sink, she says.

Read More: Are Electric Toothbrushes Better?

Men’s Health Associate Producer Janie Booth says the round, oscillating head reminds her of the tool dental hygienists use to polish teeth during a professional cleaning. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both of which are easy to pack. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long.

Booth says she’s used it for a month without recharging once. If your biggest concern is avoiding charging as much as possible, the Rev is your best bet. The battery even outperforms the Oral-B iO Series 9 and Philips Sonicare DiamondClean, both of which are roughly $300 more expensive.

I’ve used all three as my daily driver at different times, and the Rev battery lasts at least a week longer. You can expect to get at least 5 weeks from a single full charge with twice-a-day use. The rest of its offerings are pretty minimal, though, again, this will be welcomed by newcomers. It only offers three levels of intensity, but none are too strong for sensitive teeth.

However, they’re not quite as powerful as the most intense settings on Oral-B and Philips, though they are close. The Oral-B iO Series 9 offers about 10,500 oscillations per minute on its Daily Clean setting, while the Rev goes up to 9,630 oscillations per minute. Considering the $300 price difference between the two, the slight dip is a worthy trade-off.

Before I upgraded to an electric, I was a devotee of Colgate’s Active Prevention Foaming Toothbrush. The heads are as soft as they come, and the handle fits perfectly in my hand. Naturally, I was thrilled when the brand made an electric version, adding vibration to those two core features. To be clear, this is battery-powered, so it’s not rechargeable. But you also don’t need to worry about recharging it every couple of weeks. I get a little more than a month out of each set of batteries (two AAAs), so while it’s under $15 at first, I plan to spend more over time.

Still, I haven’t tried a battery-powered toothbrush that lasts that long without sputtering or losing efficiency, like Colgate’s can. It’s not the most powerful electric toothbrush, as Colgate doesn’t even list its vibrations per minute (which usually means it’s nothing to write home about). But I’ve yet to find a battery-powered toothbrush that can compete with the power of rechargeable options, so it’s inherent to the design.

No matter your background, everyone shares one truth: we all lie to our dentists about flossing. They see through it, and they roll their eyes for good reason. Daily flossing is essential, which is why Waterpik built a toothbrush with an integrated water flosser. Its all-in-one design lets you brush and floss at the same time, saving effort while leaving your teeth feeling dentist-clean.

The brush includes two intensity modes and a timer, but the standout is the built-in Waterpik. You can brush with or without the water flosser, though why skip it? While it doesn’t offer the smart features of higher-end models, the unique water flosser justifies its higher price tag. Plus, its 30,000 vibrations per minute match those of the similarly priced Zina45. In that sense, it’s like the water flosser is free.

This toothbrush offers 33,000 vibrations per minute, four custom settings, a two-minute timer, and soft, nylon bristles. It’s everything you need for a decent electric toothbrush. However, there are two features that help it stand out. For one, the magnetic USB touch charger is super convenient, making recharging as simple as any option on this list. As someone who regularly forgets to recharge his devices, I appreciate how easy this one makes the process.

It also comes with a polishing head, one of the few electric toothbrushes that do. This tiny rubber head is designed to make your teeth look smoother and shinier by focusing on surface stains and plaque removal rather than deep cleaning between teeth. I use mine after brushing, even if I brush with a separate toothbrush, to complete the full at-home dentist-level clean. It also comes with four replaceable polishing heads, so you won’t have to worry about replacing them for some time.

At first, the smaller toothbrush head on the Suri 2.0 felt less effective than the OG model, but over time, it delivers the same clean. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both designed for travel. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long. It’s the only other electric toothbrush we’ve tested that lasts over a month on a single charge, though I find it’s a couple of days shorter than the Quip Rev.

This brush delivers 33,000 vibrations per minute yet remains whisper-quiet. Its sleek case hides a UV-C light that kills 99 percent of germs on the brush head, keeping it clean wherever you take it. Plus, the head and bristles are eco-friendly, made from recyclable, plant-based cornstarch and castor oil. Overall, it’s powerful, sustainable, and travel-ready.

When choosing an electric toothbrush, you’ll need to decide between a sonic or oscillating brush head. There isn’t one right answer; it just comes down to preference.

Toothbrushes have gone smart, too. Most models include the basics—a strong motor and a built-in timer—but many now add extras like brushing modes, pressure sensors, and even AI to track your habits and coach you to improve. The right features depend on what matters most to you.

Brushing your teeth is personal, shaped by your own needs and quirks. To find the best electric toothbrushes for every sensitivity and style, we tapped a wide group of Men’s Health testers. I spoke with dentists about their go-to brands, pulled in feedback from our original 2019 guide, and compiled a list of top contenders. I then distributed these toothbrushes to writers and editors, each of whom tested them for at least a month to judge comfort, ease of use, and long-term effectiveness. Based on that feedback, here are the eight best electric toothbrushes for men in 2026.

As with manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrush heads need to be replaced every few months. Because the latter tend to be more expensive, this makes owning electric models more expensive. I recommend buying the heads in bulk when available, as this can make for pretty substantial savings. Electric toothbrushes have more nooks and crevices than their manual counterparts, which means they require a little extra daily maintenance.

This means carefully rinsing them after every use to stave off funky toothpaste and spit residue. It’s also worth actually removing the brush head from time to time to wipe the attachment point where the head meets the handle. A cotton swab or even your old toothbrush is usually enough to do the trick.

It’s tempting to just toss old toothbrushes and toothbrush heads in the trash once they’ve outlived their usefulness. But they’re actually perfect for detailed cleaning work that requires moderately stiff bristles to clean out tight spaces. Think: Shower heads, hiking boots, bathroom grout, your dishwasher filter, bird feeders—you get the idea.

#4785. The Perfect Pillow Trap: Finding Unexpected Wisdom in Discomfort

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

What if shifting your relationship with discomfort could simultaneously ease its intensity and create room for learning, growth, and transformation?

Our culture values convenience, comfort, speed, short-term gains, accumulation, and immediate relief.

When physical or psychological discomfort arises, we instinctively try to eliminate it via:

I’m not suggesting that we welcome all discomfort or simply learn to live with it. It’s important to recognize the difference among:

What I am suggesting is that sometimes, in trying so hard to find relief, we unintentionally intensify our discomfort and prolong its effects.

My relationship with physical and psychological discomfort was profoundly transformed during my initial 10-day silent meditation retreat. Participants entered the retreat center with a commitment to stay for the entire 10 days. We were required to relinquish our technology, assigned a cell-like sleeping space, and provided with a brief retreat overview.

Imagine a peaceful minimalist meditation hall, assigned meditation mats for each participant, and an outside shed filled with extra mats, pillows, and blankets. Fourteen hours of daily meditation with brief breaks. Two vegetarian meals per day. No technology, talking, reading, exercising, or familiar distractions allowed. In short, your basic meditation bootcamp.

As the days passed, my physical and psychological discomfort grew. The “silent” retreat hall included a soundtrack comprised of frequent outbursts of belching, passing gas, desperate shifting bodies, and deep sighs and moans.

Despite decades of meditation practice, I soon felt the physical and psychological strain and pain of sitting cross-legged for hours. My body was shouting “enough,” while my mind intensely revisited past challenges, failures, and unfinished business.

I had no idea how to manage the pain. During each brief break, I rummaged in the shed for the perfect combination of pillows to ease my rapidly expanding physical discomfort and psychological distress. I was determined and optimistically certain that the ideal pillow combination existed and that I would find it.

By day four, 20 pillows of various shapes and sizes crowded my meditation mat. Increasingly desperate for comfort, I fervently continued my pillow arrangement mission, unsuccessfully creating and assessing one combination after another.

None of the pillow combinations worked. My physical discomfort and psychological stress kept growing. Although I remained committed to staying for the entire retreat, I had no idea how I would make it through. And then something miraculously shifted.

On day five, my pillow quest unexpectedly gave way to releasing. My body and psyche elegantly eased into the meditation sessions. The quality of my discomfort and my relationship to it changed. During the breaks, I found myself returning my stash of pillows, one by one, to the shed.

Rather than finding the perfect pillow combination, I discovered something more powerful: Discomfort and comfort are always in flow. As my relationship with discomfort changed, my experience of it shifted, and my suffering was diminished.

Our instinct and attempts to mitigate or eliminate discomfort often serve to intensify it. We tense and adjust, ruminate, distract, seek immediate relief, make premature decisions, and attempt to control. Our vigorous efforts merely serve to intensify our suffering.

Allowing means acknowledging our experience without immediately judging it or trying to fix, change, or escape it. It does not mean resigning ourselves to our experience or even liking it.

Through the practice of active inquiry, we can observe our discomfort with curiosity:

Releasing cannot be forced. It unfolds as we loosen our attachment to a specific goal, outcome, expectation, timing, or meaning. As I naturally let go of my quest for the perfect pillow combination and sat with my discomfort, its intensity eased.

Discomfort does not automatically provide a direct path to wisdom. It can, however, provide the opportunity for understanding and transformation. Through releasing resistance to discomfort, room is created to pause, listen, and allow something better suited to emerge in our various life realms.

Growth and transformation become possible when we approach discomfort with curiosity, awareness, openness, cognitive flexibility, and a commitment to learning. Consider what various forms of discomfort invite us to explore:

At the beginning of the retreat, I naively thought the perfect combination of pillows would empower me to eradicate my discomfort. I searched, collected, experimented, and assessed. The harder I tried to control discomfort, the more powerless I felt. As I began to release control and sit with my experience, the intensity, quality, and meaning of my discomfort began to shift and transform.

How often do we try to manage life’s discomforts by accumulating “pillows”—material goods, distractions, quick fixes, expectations, control attempts?

I’m a fan of comfort, not an advocate for doing without it. My invitation is simply to notice when seeking comfort serves us and when it gets in the way of learning, growth, and transformation.

Trying to avoid discomfort at all costs can be physically and emotionally exhausting. Approaching it with curiosity, awareness, openness, flexibility, and a sense of humor about our shared humanity can create the requisite time and space for transformation.

#4784. Romesh Ranganathan, 48, Lost 44 Pounds by Keeping Fitness Simple—Here's How He Made Exercise Stick

The comedian says strength training, running and consistency—not vanity—have transformed his health.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Funny and self-deprecating on screen, Romesh Ranganathan takes his health and fitness seriously off it. He's not your typical gym-goer, though. Rather than training to build a bodybuilder's physique or hit performance milestones, his focus is on staying strong, healthy and active as he gets older—and being there for his three sons.

“I got a medical when I turned 40 as I started to worry about my own mortality, not for myself, but because of my kids,” he told On: Yorkshire Magazine. “Before, when I was going to the gym or staying on top of fitness, I'd do it for some sort of vanity reason. I've long since abandoned that and have accepted that I'm never going to look good. So the second half is about my reaction to that medical.”

Now 48, Ranganathan revealed on the Wolf & Owl podcast that he's been training more consistently in recent months. He has previously said he lifts weights three or four times a week—sometimes more if his schedule allows—while also trying to keep his daily step count high.

“I started hitting the gym for weights about three to four times a week, sometimes more if I fancied, and was trying to up my step count and cardio, but my appetite for that is a struggle,” he said in an interview with Huel.

It's an approach that has helped him lose around 44 pounds over the past few years.

Running has also become a key part of his fitness journey. After initially hating it, the comedian went on to complete the London Marathon in both 2024 and 2025.

The turning point came after one piece of simple advice.

“Running is something that people had always recommended to me. But as soon as I had a go at it, I found it unbearable. I'd go out for a run and be blowing after two minutes, then start walking, run a bit more, start blowing again. I'd come back and just feel absolutely battered,” he told Runner's World.

“Then somebody gave me the basic tip of just slowing down a little bit and getting on top of my breathing. That is the single most helpful tip I've ever had; suddenly I went from someone who couldn't face running to seeing all of the benefits of it. That's not to say that it suddenly became easy.”

#4783. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

thanks for posting. PA continues to lead the country in turning this program into actual chargers. The statewide coverage is night and day from just 2-3 years ago.

For the southeastern projects, PennDOT’s estimated schedule puts environmental reviews in November 2026 through January 2027, followed by agreement execution in January and February. Drivers will still have to wait for construction and commissioning before these awards become places to plug in.

#4782. BYD’s flagship luxury EV with 1,000+ km of range hits 4,000 sales in just 19 days

BYD wasted no time, with sales of its new flagship electric sedan reaching 4,000 in just 19 days since its launch.

With a record of more than 300,000 electric vehicles sold last month, BYD sold more EVs than the US did in the entire third quarter, combined.

A big part of the higher demand is thanks to BYD’s latest breakthrough technology, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology.

BYD began equipping vehicles with the new battery and charging tech in March, and over the past six months it has posted higher year-over-year sales growth. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 vehicles, up 6% compared to the same period in 2025.

On October 13, BYD launched the Great Han, or “Da Han” in China, the first fully electric D-segment flagship sedan in its Dynasty lineup.

Just 19 days after its launch, BYD said Great Han EV sales reached 4,000 units. At that rate, sales could reach 10,000 or more in its first full month.

With “class-beating high value,” BYD said, “it has firmly established itself in the mid-to-high-end sedan segment above 250,000 yuan,” which is about $37,500.

The Great Han is available in three variants, priced from 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000. Buyers can choose from single- or dual-motor powertrains. The standard rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Premium trim offers up to 1,008 km (626 miles) of CLTC range, while the all-wheel-drive (AWD) Flagship variant offers up to 880 km (546 miles).

All models use a 102.326 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery pack. The RWD models have a single 370 kW (496 hp) motor, while the AWD variant adds a 200 kW (268 hp) front motor for a combined 570 kW (764 hp).

Like most of its new vehicles, the Great Han has a roof-mounted LiDAR and BYD’s God’s Eye B, a more advanced version of its intelligent driving system.

The ADAS system offers safety and convenience features, including Navigate on Autopilot on highways and in cities, plus remote autonomous parking.

All variants also include premium features, such as BYD’s DiSus-A dual-chamber air suspension system, rear-wheel steering, and zero-gravity front seats.

Measuring 5,256 mm in length, 1,999 mm in width, and 1,510 mm in height, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, the Great Han is slightly bigger than the Tesla Model S and Lucid Air. It’s closer in size to the long-wheelbase Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

Thanks to BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. A full recharge (10% to 97%) takes just 9 minutes.

The Great Han joins the Great Tang SUV as the flagship sedan under BYD’s Dynasty lineup. BYD announced that Great Tang sales reached 14,000 units in October, marking four months of sales above 10,000.

#4780. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4779. Why Smart People Still Believe These 5 Myths

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Chances are, you will succumb to at least one common seasonal false belief. When you see a child queued up to see Santa having a full-blown meltdown, do you suspect excessive candy cane consumption? Maybe you insist that family members wear winter beanies because you believe most body heat escapes from the head? Have you moved a poinsettia out of a toddler's reach for fear of poisoning? If so, you are in great company, but also 100% wrong, according to science!

A dozen controlled trials show that sugar does not cause hyperactivity, the head accounts for only about 10 percent of body heat loss, and poinsettias pose no serious poisoning risks (Vreeman & Carroll, 2008). Despite what you might believe, each statement above is refuted by scientific evidence.

As I stated in my last post on popular psychology myths, the reasons why "smart" people reject facts are voluminous, but often include cultural and personal experience, inability or unwillingness to examine evidence, and herd mentality (whereby group endorsement supports believability). People also resist abandoning false beliefs when they perceive no compelling reason to change or fail to recognize the consequences of those beliefs. To fully understand how beliefs influence behavior, we must first distinguish beliefs that science can refute from those that cannot be objectively dispelled. For example, we won't debate things like how much sex is appropriate in a marriage, how much money should be contributed to charities, or whether stealing is acceptable if you are starving. Science cannot answer these types of questions. Instead, below I identify popular myths that hinder organizational performance, thinking, and decision-making, focusing primarily on motivation and achievement. I close by emphasizing that scientific understanding must remain open to revision as new evidence emerges, reflecting the evolving nature of research.

Generations of parents and educators have been conditioned to believe that offering rewards undermines the joy of doing something for its own sake. The myth suggests that paying a child to read means raising a child who never reads for fun again. The evidence tells a different story. The detrimental effects of rewards are narrow and occur only under specific conditions (Hoffman, 2025).

A 40-year meta-analysis revealed intrinsic motivation (i.e., doing things voluntarily and for pleasure) and extrinsic rewards (e.g., recognition, money, or praise) jointly predict performance, with internal drive better predicting work quality and incentives better predicting work quantity (Cerasoli et al., 2014). As I argued in The Paradox of Passion, the brain does not sort motivation into tidy "intrinsic" and "extrinsic" buckets. Rewards, whether a paycheck, praise, or a dopamine rush, covertly shape almost everything we choose to do (Hoffman, 2025). The question is not whether to use rewards, but how to use them productively.

"Follow your passion" is a motivational speaker's mantra and the foundational message in many commencement speeches. The advice implies that passion is discoverable, like buried treasure, and that finding it is the secret to a fulfilling life.

Research suggests this belief can backfire.

People who view interests as fixed and discoverable are less curious about topics outside existing interests, expect newfound passion to provide limitless motivation, and lose interest faster when work gets difficult (O'Keefe et al., 2018). In reality, passion is more often developed than discovered. It typically follows competence, effort, investment, and reward rather than preceding them (Hoffman, 2025). Waiting for passion to strike is a reliable way to wait a very long time.

Few constructs have moved from a journal to the bestseller list to school policy as quickly as “grit,” defined as passion and perseverance for long-term goals.

A meta-analysis of 88 independent samples representing 66,807 individuals found that grit's relationship with performance is modest, that it overlaps heavily with the established trait of conscientiousness, and that perseverance is what really drives long-term success (Credé et al., 2017). Persistence matters, but grit is neither new nor the secret sauce it has been marketed to be. Labeling a struggling student as "lacking grit" repackages the old claim that some people are simply unmotivated (Hoffman, 2017), using a memorable and emotionally charged term that describes someone who overcomes obstacles.

The "10,000-hour rule" suggests that intentional and sufficient practice will turn you into a bona fide expert. Talent, in this view, is optional. A meta-analysis of deliberate practice studies shows us otherwise. Dedicated practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education, and less than 1% in professions (Macnamara et al., 2014). Practice is essential, but not a guarantee of expertise. Perfect practice is far different than engagement alone. Skills can be developed, but objective feedback, strategy changes, and openness to criticism also matter.

Believing that intelligence is fixed can limit intellectual growth. After all, if you think you cannot change, why try? For decades, the antidote to fixed intelligence was a brief growth mindset intervention, often a single session designed to persuade believers that neuroplasticity means the brain can grow. This myth permeates schools as the magic solution to academic apathy. However, a meta-analysis of 63 studies with 97,672 participants found little effect of mindset training on actual achievement. Ironically, studies conducted by authors who received financial benefits from mindset consulting reported more positive findings than those without incentives (Macnamara & Burgoyne, 2023). Believing you can change is important, but a brief training session from a mindset coach is no better a solution to academic achievement than watching an infomercial and expecting to look 20 years younger by using some random face cream.

The most likely answer is “YES,” and according to research, you will continue to embrace your beliefs despite the evidence presented here. If it is any consolation, scientists are not immune to harboring false beliefs either. Several "facts" in the original version of this article have subsequently needed revision, which is exactly how good science is supposed to work. Nothing lasts forever, including some of the most well-known findings in the history of psychology research!

Cerasoli, C. P., Nicklin, J. M., & Ford, M. T. (2014). Intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives jointly predict performance: A 40-year meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(4), 980–1008.

Credé, M., Tynan, M. C., & Harms, P. D. (2017). Much ado about grit: A meta-analytic synthesis of the grit literature. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113(3), 492–511.

Hoffman, B. (2017). Hack your motivation: Over 50 science-based strategies to improve performance. Attribution Press.

Hoffman, B. (2025). The paradox of passion: How rewards covertly control motivation. Bloomsbury Academic.

Macnamara, B. N., & Burgoyne, A. P. (2023). Do growth mindset interventions impact students' academic achievement? A systematic review and meta-analysis with recommendations for best practices. Psychological Bulletin, 149(3–4), 133–173.

Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608–1618.

O'Keefe, P. A., Dweck, C. S., & Walton, G. M. (2018). Implicit theories of interest: Finding your passion or developing it? Psychological Science, 29(10), 1653–1664.

Vreeman, R. C., & Carroll, A. E. (2008). Festive medical myths. BMJ, 337, a2769.
